subsubtopic: RENTAL INCOME
speechtext: Is the government considering a change in its position of not allowing Rental Income to qualify as Income from Active Business for the purposes of the Small Business deduction and (a) if so, what are those changes (b) if not, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: RENTAL INCOME
speechtext:
The determination of whether rental income represents income from an active business is a question to be decided on the basis of the facts in each case. If the facts indicate that the rental operation is an active business, the rental income will qualify for the small business deduction under paragraph 125 (1) (a) of the Income Tax Act; otherwise, it would be treated as investment income.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF LAWYERS TO ACT ON BEHALF OF GOVERNMENT OF NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Exclusive control of all legal business of the federal government is vested in the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada by the Department of Justice Act, except non-litigious business of certain of the statutory agents of Her Majesty which are entrusted with their own funds. Cases are handled either by permanent staff of the Department of Justice or its regional offices or by the appointment of a legal agent who will act on instructions of the Department of Justice or the client department. An agent is an agent of the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada regardless of how he receives his instructions and, where he deems the circumstances to require it, he can report to, and seek instructions from, the Deputy Minister of Justice. When considering counsel for appointment as agents of the Attorney General of Canada the type of case is taken into account and a counsel's specialization in that area of the law considered before appointment is made. Further, the factor of experience in dealing with the class of subject also is taken into consideration. The Minister of Justice, under statute, has always been charged with the responsibility to appoint competent legal agents to handle civil and criminal cases on behalf of the government that are not handled directly by legal staff of the department. All governments in the past have observed the unchallenged principle that the choice of agents to act on behalf of the minister rests with him, and that the criterion for appointment is one of competence. Advice on appointment of agents is taken from numerous sources including, at times, local bar societies. The final choice of legal agents is simply a matter of judgment and there is no single set procedure for receiving recommendations. The object of receiving recommendations from various sources is to ensure that the best available counsel are known to the department should their services be required in future. The recommendation of counsel does not signify approval or authority "to act on behalf of the government" at this point of time, as a lawyer only becomes an agent of the Attorney General after a case has arisen and instructions have been issued by the Department of Justice or the client department. Regardless from what quarter a recommendation is received the test of competence is the basis for appointment.

speechtext:
Exclusive control of all legal business of the federal government is vested in the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada by the Department of Justice Act, except non-litigious business of certain of the statutory agents of Her Majesty which are entrusted with their own funds. Cases are handled either by permanent staff of the Department of Justice or its regional offices or by the appointment of a legal agent who will act on instructions of the Department of Justice or the client department. An agent is an agent of the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada regardless of how he receives his instructions and, where he deems the circumstances to require it, he can report to, and seek instructions from, the Deputy Minister of Justice. When considering counsel for appointment as agents of the Attorney General of Canada the type of case is taken into account and a counsel's specialization in that area of the law considered before appointment is made. Further, the factor of experience in dealing with the class of subject also is taken into consideration. The Minister of Justice, under statute, has always been charged with the responsibility to appoint competent legal agents to handle civil and criminal cases on behalf of the government that are not handled directly by legal staff of the department. All governments in the past have observed the unchallenged principle that the choice of agents to act on behalf of the minister rests with him, and that the criterion for
June 13, 1973

appointment is one of competence. Advice on appointment of agents is taken from numerous sources including, at times, local bar societies. The final choice of legal agents is simply a matter of judgment and there is no single set procedure for receiving recommendations. The object of receiving recommendations from various sources is to ensure that the best available counsel are known to the department should their services be required in future. The recommendation of counsel does not signify approval or authority "to act on behalf of the government" at this point of time, as a lawyer only becomes an agent of the Attorney General after a case has arisen and instructions have been issued by the Department of Justice or the client department. Regardless from what quarter a recommendation is received the test of competence is the basis for appointment.

speechtext: What percentage of the national debt is war-created?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: NATIONAL DEBT
speechtext: The net public debt is the excess of gross liabilities over net recorded assets. So defined, it is also a measure of the cumulative excess of budgetary disbursements for all purposes over budgetary receipts. It is thus not possible to apportion the cumulative deficit to particular expenditure categories. During the years of the First and Second World Wars, the net debt rose by $12.3 billion. Most of this increase was in fact attributable to the war effort.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-192, to amend the Income Tax Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the basic objectives of the measures before the House for its consideration this afternoon are twofold: they are to protect the millions of jobs that today depend directly and indirectly on maintaining the international competitiveness of our vitally important manufacturing and processing industries, and to promote the development of many hundreds of thousands of new jobs for our rapidly growing labour force in the years that lie ahead.
In a recent Toronto address, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) suggested that when the full impact of the enlarged European Common Market and the United States DISC scheme became apparent, he was "certain we will need stronger and better measures", to use his words, than those being considered by the House today to assist Canadian manufacturers and processors. I hasten to acknowledge at the outset of my remarks that the Leader of the Opposition may very well be right. It follows, I believe, that whatever may need to be done in the future to meet changing world conditions, parliament should adopt the measures we are now proposing to help our manufacturing and processing industries to meet and match the increasingly intense competition they face from foreign companies both in our own home market and in markets abroad.
When I first proposed these measures to help strengthen the structure of Canada's vitally important manufacturing and processing industries, I described them as the first major step being taken by the government to develop a coherent set of new industrial policies. It was never intended that this should be the last such step.
In my budget speech of last February, I pointed out to the House that "no one can predict the outcome of the changes now under way in the world's trading and financial system or what their impact may be on Canada's trading position". It is entirely possible, therefore, that at some stage in the future it may become apparent that additional measures are required to further bolster this sector of our economy so as to offset the adverse impact of these changes under way on the international stage.
In the meantime, however, the measures now being considered by the House provide a concrete and positive means of helping to overcome the critical problems confronting Canada's manufacturing and processing industries over the medium and longer term. The legislation
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
before the House for second reading, Bill C-192, provides for the reduction effective at the beginning of 1973 of the top rate of corporate tax on manufacturing and processing profits to 40 per cent, and the reduction of the rate on manufacturing and processing profits of smaller, Canadian-owned enterprises to 20 per cent. A companion proposal, the fast two-year write-off of equipment and machinery acquired by manufacturers and processors between May 8, 1972, and December 31, 1974, is subject to implementation through changes in capital cost allowance regulations under authority provided by parliament.
On May 29 I tabled a draft of the proposed regulations, which form an integral part of the plan put forward by the government, so that the House would be in a position to consider and debate the whole program in a meaningful and comprehensive way. As soon as parliament has approved this bill, it is the government's intention to introduce these regulations by order in council.
[ Translation]
So as to place these measures in perspective, may I remind the House that they are an integral part of the fiscal policies set forth in the last two budgets, aimed at strengthening Canada's industrial sector, encouraging strong growth in the production and employment sectors, and alleviating international inflationary pressures on our economy. Some of these measures have already been implemented through the statutes enacted by parliament early in this session. After Bill C-192 has been passed, we propose to go on to study Bill C-193, which also provides amendments to the Income Tax Act and measures already submitted dealing with changes in customs duties and sales and excise taxes.
As I have pointed out more than once, our country's production and processing sector is the greatest source of employment in industry. It provides good, relatively stable and well-paid jobs for almost two million Canadians, or one out of every four workers. No less important is the fact that it leads to the creation of an equal number of jobs in the numerous service enterprises which depend on the manufacturing and processing sectors. Thus it follows that the jobs of four million Canadians, or of one out of every two workers, depend on the maintenance of strong and well-established enterprises in Canada's manufacturing and processing sector.

As I have also emphasized, however, the manufacturing and processing sector of our economy is more exposed and more vulnerable to the forces of change under way throughout the world than any other. Over the past few years it has been adversely affected by the appreciation of the Canadian dollar in relation to United States currency, a development that has been far from offset by the depreciation of the Canadian dollar in relation to the currencies of a number of other major industrial nations because of the very heavy proportion of Canada's trade with the United States.
The recent enlargement of the European Common Market has added to the competitive threat both at home and abroad that confronts Canadian manufacturers and processors from that quarter. On the Pacific side of the world, a further challenge is proposed by the emergence of Japan as one of the new industrial giants.

June 13, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
Yet another element of competition faces Canadian manufacturers and processors as a result of various forms of export subsidies provided to resident companies by a number of other countries, one of the most critical being the substantial tax subsidies for exports made available in the past year to U.S. corporations under the DISC plan. The DISC scheme presents a three-pronged threat to the Canadian economy. It could intensify the competition that Canadian manufacturers and processors face from United States exports to our own domestic market; it could intensify the competition that Canadian manufacturers and processors face from United States companies in markets abroad; and, most important of all, it could over time result in a significant proportion of new capital investment and the accompanying new employment opportunities being located in the United States rather than in our own country.
The magnitude of the threat posed by DISC has now become fully evident with the publication by the U.S. administration of draft regulations proposing the adoption of accounting procedures, such as marginal costing, which would substantially enlarge the extent of the export tax subsidy available to many American companies. If there ever was any doubt about the potentially adverse impact of the DISC scheme on the Canadian economy, it should have been dispelled by the recent study undertaken by the Canadian Income Tax Committee of the Tax Executive Institute. The study concluded that Canadian manufacturers and processors would be placed at what it described as "a considerable disadvantage" if the measures now before the House were not implemented.
The necessity of taking steps to help our manufacturing and processing industries become strong and resilient is further reinforced by a host of uncertainties about future development around the globe. The international monetary front, for example, continues to be unsettled despite the major readjustment that has taken place in world currencies to restore the underlying economic balance between nations. In no small measure, these tremors appear to reflect uncertainties relating to political developments south of the border that touch the intangible but fundamental element of confidence. These same political developments also cloud the outlook for the passage of legislation by Congress that looks toward the further liberalization of world trade at a new round of GATT negotiations scheduled to commence this fall, as opposed to a return to increased protectionism by the world's major trading centres.
It is perfectly true, as the Leader of the Opposition suggested in the same speech in Toronto to which I referred earlier, that none of us knows for sure what the full effect of all these developments will be on Canadian manufacturers and processors. I do not, however, accept his contention that the government has made no real effort to determine what the effect will be. We have, in fact, made a great deal of effort to assess what the impact might be. But it is obviously quite impossible to estimate with any mathematical precision what effect any or all of these various elements are having now or may have in future on the growth of employment, production and capital investment in this country.
Tell us generally.

We do know, without any doubt, that the impact will be substantial. Clearly, for example, no one can say precisely what effect the disadvantage presented by the DISC scheme, if allowed to persist, would have over the years ahead in persuading companies to undertake capital investment in new plants and equipment south of the border rather than in Canada. However, it is becoming increasingly obvious to a growing number of Canadians that the danger of such a development occurring is very great, certainly too great to permit us to stand idly by while waiting to see the full extent to which the dangers become realities.

The reason for the special measures we are proposing to strengthen the base of the production sector and the transformation of our economy must be well understood. That is due to the fact that this sector is far more vulnerable to the negative effects than any other by the different elements I have just mentioned. The primary resource sector of our economy is generally very competitive on the international markets and it is increasingly so following the changes arising in the world's supply and demand. In general, that sector holds a strong position in the context of our fiscal legislation and also receives considerable help through various government programs. Most service enterprises are protected against foreign competition by their nature itself. That is why they are exposed to the negative effects resulting from increasing foreign competition to the extent that the latter impedes the expansion of Canadian manufacturing and processing enterprises on which it relies for its progress.
I should like to remind the House that those two sectors will benefit from the stepped down deductions provided each year by the tax reform, which will result in reducing the tax rate to 46 per cent in 1976. Smaller businesses owned by Canadians will benefit from a generous tax arrangement, as provided by the fiscal reform: their rate has been set at 25 per cent. Additional help is being offered smaller manufacturing and processing firms through a reduction in rate from 25 to 20 per cent, because they are just as vulnerable as big businesses to stiff foreign competition.

What we are proposing, therefore, are concrete measures to deal with a concrete problem. They will have their greatest effect over the medium and long term, matching the medium and long-term nature of the threat that appears to confront Canada's manufacturing and processing industries. I am confident, however, that these measures are already playing a part and will continue to play a part over the months immediately ahead in stimulating a resurgence of capital investment by manufacturers and processors to modernize and expand their productive capacity-an opinion that is shared by the Economic Council at home and the OECD abroad. Noteworthy, too, is the strong endorsation of these measures by the treasurer of Ontario in his last budget.
The survey of private and public investment published last April forecast a 9 per cent increase in manufacturing

investment after two years of declining outlays, an estimate that may well turn out to be too low given parliamentary approval of these measures and the strong upsurge currently evident in our economy.
Some firms undoubtedly have already been encouraged to undertake new capital investment as a result of the measures announced in the budget last May, or are in the process of doing so. There is, however, a good deal of evidence that a number of companies are prepared to press ahead with major new capital projects once the legislation now before the House receives parliamentary approval, creating a significant number of new job opportunities in the process.
The proposed reduction in the tax burden borne by Canadian manufacturers and processors is designed to assist them to meet increasingly intense foreign competition in a variety of ways: to increase the efficiency of their operations and lower costs; to undertake more research so as to develop new and better products and technologies; to finance increased capital investment both to modernize their operations and to expand productive capacity and employment; and to increase their price competitiveness with foreign producers both at home and abroad.
One of our major national goals in Canada, and one of the major objectives of government policies, is to achieve a better balance of industrial developments in all parts of the country so as to provide a growing number of stable, well paying and satisfying jobs for Canadian workers. We Canadians have never been content to remain hewers of wood and drawers of water. In all parts of Canada, and especially in the eastern and western regions of the country, an increasingly intense effort is being made by governments at all levels to broaden industrial development, to extend production beyond the raw and semi-processed stage to the output of fully manufactured or processed goods for sale across Canada and around the world.
We want to encourage more advanced processing and refining of metals in this country, for example, and greater use of such metals for the production of manufactured or fabricated goods here. We want to make greater use of our extensive petroleum reserves to provide the foundation of expansion of the Canadian petrochemical industry. Broadening of our industrial base, in turn, will help to promote further expansion of the multiplicity of service industries which have become essential in a modern economy to support those sectors that produce hard goods. By increasing the after-tax rate of return on investment, these measures will help to achieve these national objectives by encouraging the establishment in many parts of the country of new manufacturing and processing industries and of supporting service industries.
I recognize that some members of this House have expressed misgivings about the effectiveness of these measures in achieving their intended purpose. As I told the House when I introduced the ways and means motion on which the legislation is based, I am anxious to do everything reasonably possible to meet the legitimate concerns that have been expressed about various aspects of these measures without impairing their effectiveness in achieving our objectives.
I recalled then that in my budget speech of February, 1973, I informed the House that the government intended
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
to establish a new procedure to monitor the effect of these measures in strengthening our manufacturing and processing industries. This review procedure would assess the effect of both the reduction in the corporate tax rate and the rapid write-off of machinery and equipment acquired by manufacturers and processors to the end of 1974. I proposed in the February budget that a report assessing the effectiveness of these measures, based on detailed information gathered from 1,000 individual companies and an in-depth study of some 200 of the largest corporations, be submitted to the House by the end of 1974. The submission of this report would coincide with the completion of the thorough examination which the government proposed to make of the entire capital cost allowance.
In a further effort to meet the concerns of some hon. members, I advised the House in my statement on May 29 that the government would submit an interim report to parliament by April 1 of next year providing as factual and objective an analysis as possible of the impact of these corporate measures on the manufacturing and processing sector during the early months they were in operation.
This interim report will be based on the responses to a questionnaire to be sent to around 1,000 manufacturing and processing companies representing all regions of the country, all industrial sectors and virtually all sizes of firms. In-depth interviews will also be held with some 200 of the largest corporations and around 50 small and medium sized manufacturing and processing companies. Information about the impact of the measures in encouraging the establishment of new enterprises will be obtained through the contacts with industry maintained by my own department, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Through the extensive examination of this relatively large sample it will be possible to arrive at some estimates about their direct impact on the manufacturing and processing sector as a whole. Subsequent computer analyses of the results should also make it possible to make some reasonable estimate of the secondary effect of the measures on other areas of the economy.
I realize, of course, that it is no more possible to gauge precisely the extent to Which these measures serve their intended purpose than it is to gauge precisely the full extent of the threat they are intended to meet. I am confident, however, that the monitoring procedure will make it possible to prepare an interim report by next April that will provide a reliable indication of the early impact of these measures and that a still better picture will be provided through subsequent reports.
Coupled with the undertaking given by the government to submit an interim report on the outcome of the review and monitoring procedure that is being put into effect is a clause in the bill now before the House providing an opportunity by law for formal consideration of these measures by parliament after March 31, 1974. On the motion of 60 or more members calling for either termination of the reduced rate of taxation proposed for manufacturers and processors or for some reduction in its scope, the House would be required to debate the proposal within a period of 15 days. If the motion were approved, with or without amendment, the Minister of Finance would forthwith take such steps as are necessary in order that a measure giving

June 13, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
effect to the motion may be placed before the House without delay. At the committee stage, Mr. Speaker, I will address myself to the point that this parliamentary review, if ever initiated, will be meaningful and susceptible of a conclusion in this House.
No tax measure can be considered to be enacted for all time, particularly in a parliament made up of minorities. They must always be subject to change from time to time to meet changing conditions. Under all the circumstances, I do not consider it inappropriate to give parliament an opportunity to consider whether these very important measures are working effectively and whether their continuation is justified by future circumstances. It may well be, and I believe it probable, that parliament and the country will be so convinced of the effectiveness of these measures that the special provision to review will not be invoked.
I am confident that Canadian manufacturers and processors will make use of these measures in a way that serves our national objectives. I am sure they are all too well aware of the multiple threats confronting them and of the essential need to strengthen their position in order to survive and prosper in an increasingly competitive world. At the same time, however, I expect that the manufacturing and processing companies will recognize that an added onus is placed on them by the monitoring process and the provision establishing the opportunity for parliamentary review. The Canadian people and the Canadian parliament are going to be watching closely. They will want to be satisfied that these companies are making good use of the improvement in their financial resources to strengthen their competitive position, to increase capital investment and, above all, to create new employment opportunities. While shareholders must receive a fair and reasonable return on their investment over time if an enterprise is to remain viable, the purpose of this legislation is certainly not to provide them with a bonanza, as I am sure manufacturers and processors are well aware.
I would like to touch briefly on some of the additional concerns or criticisms that have been raised in various quarters during the course of the public debate over these proposals. Because of the particularly strong upsurge in the economy during the past six months and the substantial recovery that has taken place from the depressed profit position of Canadian industry generally, the suggestion is made that the reduction in the tax burden of manufacturers and processors has now become unnecessary. Nothing could be further from the truth. The current improvement in the position of Canadian manufacturers and processors is very welcome, but it in no way lessens the imperative need to strengthen the underlying structure of these industries to enable them to meet and match the increasingly intense competition from foreign companies in markets both at home and abroad that can be expected over the medium and longer term.
It is sometimes contended that the measures will be of little benefit to the slower growth regions of Canada where the primary resource industries have a more predominant economic role. The fact is that many such regions are now giving the highest priority to the development of secondary industry because of an increasing

awareness that excessive reliance on primary resources in the past has been one of the major causes of the slow growth of production, employment and incomes in such areas. I might point out that manufacturing grew by 11 per cent in the Atlantic provinces during the period 1966 to 1971, compared with a national growth averaging less than 2 per cent. These measures can play an important part in helping to reinforce this trend.
The measures will be of significant assistance to smaller Canadian manufacturers and processors who stand to benefit both from the fast two-year write-off on new machinery and equipment and from the reduction in their tax rate from 25 per cent to 20 per cent. The establishment of new enterprises will also be encouraged by the increased opportunity that will be made available to business to compete and operate profitably.
The measures have sometimes been criticized on the ground that they would provide significant benefit to foreign-controlled manufacturing and processing firms in Canada. The hard and unescapable fact, however, is that the jobs of a million or more workers provided directly or indirectly by such corporations today are just as much in jeopardy as those provided through companies that are domestically owned and controlled. As I said in my budget speech last February, I am sure these workers would not thank this parliament if it failed to take steps to counter the threat to their jobs because of some misguided sense of extreme nationalism. I have always said that we have to move toward greater control of our economy, and I mean this, but in a way and at a pace that does not jeopardize Canadian jobs.
A contrary concern that has been expressed is that the benefit provided to subsidiaries in Canada of U.S. corporations could be reduced or negated by new tax measures proposed by the United States. At the moment that remains no more than a hypothetical possibility. It is difficult to determine with any precision what impact the measures as proposed might have in relation to U.S. subsidiaries in Canada, and impossible to anticipate what measure, if any, might finally be approved by the U.S. Congress. We are following this situation very carefully through our contacts in Washington. It may be that what eventually emerges will require a response on our part. In my judgment, however, we would be extremely ill-advised to be deterred by hypothetical possibilities in the future from taking action to deal with the very real problems that confront us right now.
I am not going to deal now at any length with the allegations about corporate rip-offs such as have persuaded the New Democratic Party to oppose this and virtually all other measures of assistance to Canadian industry. Members of that party have become so blinded to hard reality by the glittering rhetoric of their leader, a throw back to an earlier era in Canadian industrial history, that they can no longer recognize, as they did only a year ago, the critical dangers confronting Canadian manufacturers and processors, dangers that are of very pressing concern to their close allies in the Canadian Labour Congress. The hollowness of the rhetoric of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) was illustrated within recent days when he reiterated his often-repeated contention that government programs and policies to assist Canadian indus-

try have done nothing to create employment in Canada in the past and will do nothing in the future. But it should be clearly evident that we must be doing something right in this country, Mr. Speaker, because the fact is that for several years Canada's increase in employment has far exceeded that of any nation in the industrialized world.
Between 1965 and 1970, the most recent period for which comprehensive international statistics are available, there were 1,300,000 new jobs created in Canada. That was 400,000, or 50 per cent more than the absolute increase in employment of all 15 countries then belonging to the European Economic Community and the European Free Trade Area combined, an area that has a population 13 V4 times larger than Canada's. In relative terms, employment in Canada during that period increased 57 per cent faster than in the United States, twice as fast as in Japan and 27 times as fast as in the 15 European nations taken together.
Hear, hear!

I could read those figures as well; they are also a credit to Canada. Although more current international comparisons are not available, there is every reason to believe that the rate of increase in employment in Canada has continued to exceed that of every other industrialized nation during recent years.

This happens to be a fact. During the past eight months alone, seasonally adjusted employment has been increasing at a faster rate than ever before in our history.

It is not surprising that the leader of the New Democratic Party chooses to ignore these realities, given the fact that they totally undermine the very foundation of the platform on which he has decided to make his political stand.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat the strongly held conviction that I expressed to the House in my last budget:
What is at stake is not the welfare of the corporations and their shareholders. At stake is the welfare of every Canadian. At stake

are hundreds of thousands of jobs that today depend on our manufacturers staying in business and retaining their workers. At stake also are hundreds of thousands of good steady jobs in the manufacturing sector and supporting industries that will be required in future across Canada for our new workers. It is critical that we should all have a clear understanding of what is at issue. That is why I am committed and the government is committed to these measures.

We have had a lot of this in the question period during the past few days. However, the minister set one record: if the beginning of the debate on second reading of this bill can be considered as the first stirring of life in the measure, then there has been a period of political gestation with respect to the budget bill-the longest ever known in Commonwealth parliamentary history. It is one year, 36 days, four hours and 441/2 minutes since the minister introduced his proposal to a waiting and expectant House of Commons and country, saying, in effect, as he did so: This bill will shortly be brought down. This is what the country wants. There will be no time lost. This is what you want to have. This is what I, Dr. Turner, think you need, and you will have it shortly.
Mr. Speaker, I think all of us in this House have common objectives. We want to do the things that need to be done for the people of Canada-provide jobs, stability and a good life. I do not think there is any distinction among members in any part of this House in regard to those objectives. However, we have different methods of attempting to achieve them. Today the minister talked about these measures being promoted because, in his own words, "of the need to find millions of jobs". He told us about what he said in the budget speech in this House, and there was some mention of the Speech from the Throne.
It was all very healthy and very interesting, and some very fine statements were made during the course of those debates. But, Mr. Speaker, how can we rely upon the good faith, upon the bona fides of this government when we have a government and a minister who in their twisting and turning and vocal and intellectual acrobatics have succeeded in imposing a measure of deception upon this House and the country?
Hear, hear!

That will make up for some of the defects in his past conduct.

We are being asked today to debate a bill that will introduce what the Minister of Finance has called the "first major step in the development of a new industrial strategy". In the more than 13 months that have elapsed since the promise of that first major step we have progressed sufficiently to know that we should not wait with bated breath for a second major step, for there might not ever be one. Apparently we were so reckless in starting out that we got hopelessly mired with the first stride- rather like the muskeg you sometimes find in the Peace River country.
Could it be that the government does not believe in rushing things? This is not a rushing government, Mr. Speaker. That would at least partially explain the delay in bringing these corporate tax measures before the House. First promised in the budget of May, 1972, these measures were supposed "to protect existing jobs and provide wellpaying new jobs for Canadians". I am quoting from the minister's statement. Yet though job creation, as the minister never tired of telling us ad nauseam, was the first priority, and though unemployment was well in excess of 6 per cent, it took the government until now, when the economy is supposedly booming and must now be restrained, to attempt to put into effect these measures that are intended to stimulate the economy.
These measures were also supposed to help Canadian manufacturing and processing firms to withstand foreign competition. "It is a matter of some urgency", the Minister of Finance was declaring about six months after his first budget, "that all of the tax measures proposed in the budget should be given early consideration and approval by parliament." Well, it took the Minister of Finance seven more months, because of an inept legislative program by this government and this cabinet, before he brought these "urgent" measures before the House for consideration. All I can say is, thank God the land is strong, for God only knows the state we would be in today if we had to rely only on the management and speed of this government.
When reductions and accelerated write-offs for manufacturing and processing industries were first introduced, the position taken by this party was that though the intent of the minister-to improve the ability of Canadian business to compete both domestically and abroad-was honourable, the method of going about it was exceedingly defective. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in the course of the debate following that budget stated clearly our objections to the measures as introduced, and I quote as follows from the statement of the Leader of the Opposition:
-the proposal of the minister falls far short of being an effective tool to expand Canadian manufacturing and processing. I also point out that there is really nothing here to encourage Canadians to invest more of their money in their economy in order to play a bigger part in the ownership of that Canadian economy in the future. I also point out to the Minister of Finance, that, in so far as he claims that reducing these taxes will make these corporations more profitable, this is just as attractive to foreign capital as it is to Canadian capital. There is nothing in the minister's proposal which encourages Canadians as such to acquire a bigger share of the economy in the future.
Those words are recorded on page 2266 of Hansard of that year. Last October, pursuing the course of consistency

which is the trademark of the Leader of the Opposition, he said, when asked what he would do with respect to the corporate tax proposals: "I would think we would be under some moral obligation to carry them through for the time being at least." Our position was then, and has been since, that there were sufficient doubts concerning the equity and efficacy of the proposed corporate tax changes to warrant their not being made a permanent feature of our tax structure.
Firstly, the proposed measures offer little or no aid to those companies which are in greatest need of aid, since the availability of their benefits is predicated on high profits. Accordingly, these measures, the primary justification of which is increased international competition, will help least these companies which suffer most severely from such competition. They offer no encouragement to start new business, nor do they improve the capacity of young companies to survive.
Secondly, most benefits from the reduced tax will accrue to foreign-controlled corporations which account for more than 60 per cent of all manufacturing profits in Canada. It is doubtful that the tax cuts will have a perceptible influence on the behaviour of these corporations.
Thirdly, the proposed corporate tax changes are inequitable and maladjusted. The intended aid will accrue primarily to firms in central Canada, where four-fifths of manufacturing firms are located. This is the area where, so the minister and his advisers maintain, employment is already so high that any additional stimulus might fuel inflation. The measures will do little to help Canada's most disadvantaged regions which need economic stimulus the most.
Finally, the measures are discriminatory. For one thing, they do not apply to the more labour-intensive service industries which employ two-thirds of all Canadian workers and are frequently subject to intensive international competition. It is perhaps true that a strong manufacturing sector will help the service industry as well, but there is no reason why the spin-offs cannot work the other way as well. A more dynamic service sector can increase the demand for manufactured goods and lower costs of services to manufacturing. Studies by the economic community in fact show that the manufacturing sector performs best when the rest of the economy is also strong.
While the government proposals will reduce taxes for manufacturers and processors, they will increase them for all other businesses, small and large. As well, as Dominion Stores Limited pointed out in submissions to the Commons food prices committee, the proposed tax reduction will favour service enterprises which are vertically integrated, giving them an unfair competitive advantage. Because of all these objections and doubts we refused, as the Leader of the Opposition said, to give our unconditional support to the tax measures as proposed by the government.
The Leader of the Opposition indicated the condition for our support. He made it plain both in speeches in this House and outside this House. The minister, as I said before, has actually surrendered the position which he originally took and has adopted the logical and sensible attitude of the Leader of the Opposition and my party. The Minister of Finance himself, while asking us to approuve
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
measures that would cost the treasury $500 million, has presented no evidence to show that his measures will in fact work. We have only his optimism to guide us-and his optimism must, I submit, be subject to certain scrutiny. The closest he never came to providing such evidence was in a statement following the budget when he said, according to a press release of May 8, 1972, "I hope they use it"- meaning the money made available by the tax cuts-"for increased growth, for new competitiveness, for new jobs." He put forward no measures to ascertain that business would act according to his hope, yet his proposals were offered for adoption for all time, forever and ever, thus emphasizing the fact that, to use his own words, "they are permanent incentives to the manufacturing and processing industries in this country." Those words, again, are taken from his press conference of May 8, 1972. It is this sort of permanence that the leader of my party, in view of the doubts just expressed, was not prepared to accept. We were not prepared to accept the conditions being laid down by the minister.
So that there could be no misunderstanding, on March 21, 1973, the Leader of the Opposition advised the Minister of Finance that my party "will not support a budget bill provision making this special reduced rate a permanent feature of the Canadian tax system." The Minister of Finance went out of his way, as he had done so often in the past, to demonstrate his disagreement with the Conservative proposal. The minister is obviously a slow learner, or likes eating his own words. That is an unacceptable diet. In any event, two days following the statement of the Leader of the Opposition, in a speech before the Canadian Club of Toronto the Minister of Finance declared:
I have examined Mr. Stanfield's statement to the press on the subject of corporate tax measures and I am not moved to change what I have said to you today.
That was on March 23. On May 29, the same minister made the following announcement in this House, as recorded at page 4198 of Hansard:
-it is my intention to put before this House by April 1 of next year an interim report based on the review and monitoring procedure which I described earlier. This will give members an early opportunity to begin to assess the results of these measures on the basis of facts and figures. Members will also have an opportunity to make constructive suggestions before the final report is submitted by the end of 1974.
In this context, the government will include in the legislation a provision whereby parliament will have a fresh opportunity to consider the incentive measures. Upon the request of 60 members of this House, and after the measures have been in force for a reasonable period of time, namely, after April 1, 1974-
That was only three months beyond the period which the Leader of the Opposition suggested this party would agree to. A difference of three months was not that large that we could not go along with the proposal. The minister continued:
-the government will take the steps necessary to provide an early occasion for this House to re-examine these tax incentives and, if the House so decided, the measures would be withdrawn thereafter in whole or in part.
The minister has now come full circle: instead of offering measures that are to be permanent and have no need to be watched, he has now offered incentives which will be closely monitored and will have to justify their existence or else be terminated. It is what the Conservative Party

I know there are high-minded gentlemen opposite who are more concerned about the welfare of the country than their own defeat. We do not see any difference there.
Much will depend on what happens in committee. The minister indicated today that he had some doubts in his mind. There have been consultations with the minister with regard to the fears we expressed about the doubtful quality of the review process. However, this is a new subject. Apparently the government has at long last recognized the utility of the House of Commons. The Minister of Finance in his treatment of this measure, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in bringing forward his resolution the other day, have suddenly recalled the existence of the House of Commons and have remembered that it serves a useful function.
I would commend their course of conduct to some of the minister's cabinet colleagues, such as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras). He is dealing with problems to do with immigration and with the Unemployment Insurance Commission resulting from a silly set of bureaucratic directives that were sent out by those who do not understand the problems in these areas. I suggest to the minister that he bring before the House the problems which have been created. This House has the capacity to deal with them. In this House there is accumulated wisdom far beyond that of the minister and his civil servants for dealing with the serious and difficult problems which the government itself has created. I am speaking not only on my own behalf but on behalf of the members of my party, and particularly on behalf of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) who has kept a close eye on what the minister has been doing. It is about time the House of Commons did what it is supposed to do and dealt with those problems itself.
After second reading this bill will move into committee. The minister has already indicated a reasonable degree of flexibility on one issue and I hope he will continue. I do not need to outline the obvious defects which exist in the review process which the minister has set out, such as the question of time and the question of concluding debates. I hope the minister will be reasonable.
No amendments can be moved on second reading; at this stage it is impossible for us to put forward our suggestions in this regard. I hope the minister will be guided by the very sensible advice he received from the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and during the course of the committee hearings in this House will produce a workable and sensible review mechanism. If that is the case, quite a few of the minister's troubles may well be over, at least for the time being.
I now come to the monitoring procedure. When the minister bared these tax cuts to a waiting world 13 months ago he declared them to be:
-medium and long term in their nature and structural in the impact. They are also intended as a permanent incentive.
However, when he presented his budget on February 19 this year he had obviously lost his confidence in their efficacy because he told us he wanted a monitoring procedure to assess the effect of these corporate measures on prices and jobs. We can only hope that the experts assigned this task are more adept than their colleagues in the finance department who apparently were out nearly $1 billion in their estimates but still retain their jobs. Let us hope, too, that the minister approaches the implementation of this proposal with more determination and finesse than his colleague responsible for consumer affairs who has succeeded in confusing parliament, the country, consumers and industry with his devious twists and turns as he grapples with his "Bird-watching" Food Price Review Board.
It is nice to know the government accepts proposals of the Conservative Party-and this is not only because our proposals are good. On October 30 last the government received a very good kick in that portion of its anatomy especially designed for the receipt of corporal punishment. This has prompted them to be much more reasonable. We have made a number of proposals. Some are included in this legislation. There was the indexing of the income tax rates to the cost of living. The minister has come full circle there and has accepted the proposals of the Leader of the Opposition despite the fact that in Truro, Nova Scotia, of all places, on June 6, 1972, the minister made these solemn commitments:
I would like to deal more specifically now with Mr. Stanfield's proposal to tax personal incomes based on constant dollars. While the Conservative leader alleged that the federal government has a vested interest in inflation (in contrast to earlier accusations that the government was too zealous in trying to combat it), the fact of the matter is that the government is one of the chief victims of inflation because it has only limited scope in offsetting its own sharply rising costs. The government must continue to pay its bills in current dollars. The only way it could maintain its revenues to pay for existing services under the kind of constant-dollar tax scheme proposed by Mr. Stanfield would be by progressively increasing personal income tax rates. This was acknowledged by Mr. Stanfield himself in reply to questions I put to him on the floor of the House during the course of the debate.
What a whale of a difference an election makes! This may not be completely relevant but I point it out so that the minister will maintain this position of flexibility. It is much better for the country. The question of capital gains tax on family farms has been accepted by the government. There is also the small business legislation just introduced by the government, as well as the personal income tax reduction. Just the other day the government saw fit to accept some very sensible conclusions put forward by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) which improved the housing bill. It is still a bit of a mess but at least it has been improved.
Hear, hear!

I wish to say a few words to my friends in the New Democratic Party. The hon. member for York South will be replying shortly. I anticipate what he will say. Among

other things, the hon. member will be getting ready to drag out of cold storage and dust off his attack on corporate welfare bums. Like Don Quixote, supported by his assorted Sancho Panzas he will put on his rusty armour and gallop madly in all directions. However, some of his thunder may well be muted by the very extraordinary circumstances surrounding the mechanics and the detail of the presentation of this and accompanying legislation, the division of the bills, the type of review procedure, the timing of the bills, the device used in connection with quick write-offs, and so on.
I recall the grins on the faces of members of the cabinet the day the minister made his announcement and the Leader of the Opposition responded. There were grins of relief on the faces of the minister, the Prime Minister, the government House leader and my friends to the left. This suggested that the two parties drew together in a common political cause calculated to keep the Liberals in power in pursuance of their belief, which somehow the NDP seems to have accepted, that they, the Liberals, have a divine right to rule and will engage in any kind of political chicanery to that end. This debate will also permit the NDP to have an opportunity to stand and vote against the government. I know they have been waiting for this for a long time. They have been very frustrated because of their inability to vote against the government. This device was worked out between the two parties to enable this course to be followed.
They have been what is commonly known as shacking up.

I hope that remark will not be credited to me, Mr. Speaker. It will be welcomed by some of the disillusioned followers of the New Democratic Party in the country who have been watching with dismay and regret the stance the NDP have taken in the House so far. It is such a pitiful, palpable device and is so self-evident that it will not fool the people of Canada. It has not succeeded in fooling them, as the Gallup poll published today indicates.
It was common knowledge around the hill and in the press gallery some time before the Minister of Finance made his statement and announced his scheme that the two parties had a common cause in this regard. There is no question about it. They have a perfect right to do so, but they have to stand by the consequences. I do not know exactly what input the NDP had in the Minister of Finance's changes and in the method he used to approach the conundrum, but it will take very powerful evidence to convince me there was not some liaison to allow them both to get out of a very difficult situation and, hopefully, to draw together against Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition whom they both regard as their common enemy and most dangerous threat in this parliament.
Oh, oh!

This will be a day for the New Democratic Party. I understand this, as they have helped set the rules under which they are debating this measure and undoubtedly collaborated to that extent. But let me tell the Minister of Finance that tomorrow will be another day and another vote. Next week there will be another day and

another vote, and next year there will be another day and another vote. I suggest to the government that there will be an election one of these days, when the government and the New Democratic Party will be called upon to give an account of their conduct in this House and of this illicit relationship they have had together. I suggest that this will be a day when the god of election battles will require a very stern accounting from hon. gentlemen opposite and to my left.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot of talk about minority government. Minority government can work. It has worked in the past and will work again. But not a minority government principally composed of an ailing, impotent and ineffective group whose record eight months after the election and after almost six months of parliament has been barren of result in the past and empty of promise for the future. Some day people will be asking hon. friends to my left why they exposed the good people of Canada to the tricks of these artful dodgers of the political world.

Mr. Speaker, we have just listened to a scenario which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) read, and I like him well enough to suggest that he might even have written it, though I am not sure.

speechtext: Parts of it, the good parts.

Let me tell him that all of his scenario about the NDP and the Liberals having discussed the thing now before us-and I call it a "thing" quite deliberately-is so much hogwash, and he knows it. When he attempts to say the kind of thing he has said, he at least has the decency to smile, which is a form of honesty on his part that I appreciate.
Before I go any further let me point out that it is obvious that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the government learned that we would under no circumstances support the corporate income tax cut and fast write-off provisions, they then looked around to see what they could do in order to survive, since we made it clear to them that, whatever the consequences might be, we would vote against this measure.
It was very easy for the government to find a way. All the Minister of Finance had to do was to propose some kind of monitoring or review mechanism, put a date to it that was not far beyond December 31, 1973, and he would feel quite confident that the Conservative Party would then have the face-saving device that they needed so as to do what they intended to do all the time. When the hon. member for Peace River talks the rubbish he has just talked, he knows darned well that there has been much more collusion between his party and the Minister of Finance on this issue than there could have been in any discussions we had with the minister.
I do not want to spend too much time on the speech of the hon. member for Peace River because I want to deal with the bill, but the hon. member's speech contained some very valid and serious criticisms of the bill. He said it was discriminatory, that it would not do any good, that it would serve foreign-controlled corporations more than Canadian corporations. At the end of it I expected him to

June 13, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
say, "In view of this, we will oppose the bill". But no, Mr. Speaker. The logical conclusion to his criticisms was something that he could not utter because his party cannot afford to oppose corporate concessions today any more than it has been able to afford them in the past. Because their financial resources might dry up, if not wholly at least partially, the hon. member for Peace River had to go easy in this kind of situation.
It was very significant that the Minister of Finance, when making the proposal regarding the monitoring and review procedures, placed in the bill the provision that 60 members were required to sign a petition before a resolution to reconsider the matter could come before parliament. Not 20 members, or 25, which would have made certain that there would be a demand for a review, but 60 members. The Minister of Finance knew perfectly well that if the number were high enough the Conservatives would have to put a resolution on the order paper, and that that resolution would never get on the order paper.
Let us look at the facts the way they are, rather than letting the Tories attempt to play their own game. I am certain that whatever the Gallup poll may say today, or whatever it said two months ago when it had us up and the Tories down, we have taken the right position in this parliament. What is more, we intend to continue to take the same position and to try our utmost to make this parliament work. But not at the expense of something with which basically we disagree.
The Minister of Finance very kindly referred-I suppose he intended it as a compliment-to my "glittering rhetoric" which has blinded our party. I am sorry I cannot return the compliment; I can only say to him that his exuberant verbosity cannot take the place of thinking, try as he might. In fact, I was almost going to say that his soporific verbiage does not make the bill any better now than it was before he spoke.
Let me deal with some of the economic factors here. The fact is that what the minister is now doing makes no sense whatever in terms of Canada's economy. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, of two things. The minister said during his February budget-I do not have his exact words but I am sure I am not misrepresenting him-that he made more disposable income available to Canadians through the individual income tax cut, at a level that would not be too harmful to the economy, and we approved of this. Instead of making a higher individual income tax cut and putting another $500 million at the disposal of the ordinary taxpayer, the minister said, "I have to keep the disposable income in the hands of the Canadian purchaser at a level that will not heat up the economy too much".
Then remember too, Mr. Speaker, that the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have been saying for days now that it is important to allow interest rates to go up, because the economy of Canada was getting to the point where the demand for loans is too high and the heating up of the economy is becoming dangerous from the point of view of inflation.
He hesitates to give any more to the individual taxpayer. He knows of the higher interest rates and the higher costs to ordinary Canadian purchasers of homes and

goods, but he hesitates not one whit to heat up the Canadian economy by giving the corporations a further $500 million concession in tax exemptions. That, Mr. Speaker, is economic lunacy. If the economy of Canada has reached the point where it is heating up too much and you have to be careful not to heat it up any more, what conceivable sense does it make to give more money to the corporations, allegedly to have higher investment, and heat up the economy more?
What kind of sense does it make for the Conservative Party to say that because the government has given us three months and we will have a review, therefore they will support this proposal and vote for it on second reading? That is the situation if I understood the hon. member for Peace River correctly.
It is not merely the injustices and the inequities which are introduced by this measure which bother us. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, it is economically invalid at this time in Canada's development. The minister boasted about the high increase in employment in Canada. Let me remind you that when you start low enough you have nowhere to go but up. When the government in its 1968-69 policies forced employment down, then unemployment went up, so that the situation could not be anything else when unemployment is reduced than to have employment increase. The minister really has no reason to boast about it.
When the minister compares Canada's record in the realm of employment and unemployment with Japan or some countries in Europe, then it really does become rather ridiculous because anyone who knows anything at all about the economies of Japan, West Germany and, until very recently, Britain, or Sweden knows perfectly well that they have not only had full employment in those countries but have imported labour-in West Germany to the extent of 1,500,000 workers. When everybody is employed, how can you have further increases in employment? These comparisons are really not worthy of the Minister of Finance and are patently wrong.
We oppose this bill, not because of any glittering rhetoric or any nonsense of that sort but because we are convinced, through the history of this country, that these concessions do not help the economy. They never create many jobs, if any. They merely serve to increase the profits of corporations and increase the amount of deferred taxes of large corporations. That is the result of these fast write-offs. Let us spend a moment on the fast write-offs which are part of this package. There is absolutely no evidence in the history of this country to show that these fast write-offs have done anything for the economy except to make the foreign-owned corporations more powerful and more able to buy up the rest of Canada's economy. That is all they have ever done.
There is no evidence that these fast write-offs have created anything except a volume of available investment capital to the corporations which they can use without having to pay any interest on them. These increases in the interest rates, which the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister say are necessary in order to meet the international situation and to lower the size of the demand for loans, do not accomplish what is claimed for them.
The fact is that anyone who studies Canada's economy knows perfectly well that with the retained earnings in
June 13, 1973

the hands of the large corporations, many of them foreign-owned, with the amount of deferred taxes, and with their available resources, they need not go to the capital market except when we undertake a nonsense proposal like the James Bay project or the Mackenzie valley pipeline. That kind of proposal requires the kind of investment where people have to go to the market to find the money. For the regular expansion of General Motors, General Electric, Ford, Westinghouse or Domtar these corporations have enough in their retained earnings, in their depreciation reserves and in their deferred taxes; they do not have to go to the money market to carry out their expansion.
The only people who are hurt by higher interest rates are the small Canadian businessmen and the ordinary Canadian purchaser of a house or any kind of durable goods he may require in his home. They are the only people hurt, not the large corporations. The fast write-off has proven historically to be of no value in the creation of jobs. I cannot understand how the Minister of Finance and his advisers in the ministry of finance think, and I do not know what they use for thinking. I do not know why they think the rest of the people in Canada are so unintelligent they will buy their proposals.
If the fast write-offs, the capital cost allowances, do play any part in the job market, they necessarily and logically play the part of reducing the numbers of jobs, not increasing them. New industry cannot take advantage of the fast write-off. If it does, it needs a constant flow of capital investment and capital purchases in order to retain deferred taxes. So what you are doing is saying to the existing manufacturing firm and the existing processing firm, "You can buy new equipment and write it off in two years. You can set aside"-I don't know how many millions or hundreds of millions of dollars in deferred taxes- "and you have capital without interest for a long time." What will that industry do? I suggest it will change its obsolescent equipment for new, labour-saving equipment and will be able to produce more, with less labour and fewer jobs than at this time. How in heaven's name can anyone sensibly and logically argue that fast write-offs will produce jobs in Canada, when in fact they reduce the demand for jobs by the introduction of labour-saving devices if they do anything at all?
I looked at the investment survey for 1973 carried out by Statistics Canada and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. We must remember that the offer of fast write-offs was made on May 8, 1972, but actually capital investment in 1972 declined from 1971. This did not play the slightest part in increasing the investment of those firms so far as the statistics are concerned. I have no doubt that to the extent this did anything, it played a part in increasing profits.
Now we come to the corporation income tax cut. Here the Minister of Finance really plays the fiddle. Ever since I started studying economics a long time ago, back in 1927-28 when I entered university, I have heard the same tune played by the traditional economists: If you want to help the economy, cut the taxes of the corporation. If there is any logic to that argument of the Minister of Finance, this country would be best off it we had no corporate income tax at all. That is the logic of his proposition. Every time I have listened to a budget-all but one-I
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
have heard this argument. It is significant that the one exception was the budget of February 19, 1973. Significantly enough, the government knew that if that budget contained any corporate concessions, this party would vote against it and the government would go down. Significantly enough, the budget of February 19, 1973, contained not a wink of a concession to corporations in this country and that is why we were able to support it.
Every time there has been a budget we have had some kind of concession made to the corporations of this country such as fast write-offs, income tax credits, and for the wealthy people dividend tax credits. All these things were supposed to strengthen the economy and increase the amount of Canadian ownership. The fact is that with the fast write-offs, income tax concessions and the tax dividend credits, in 1969, 1970 and 1971 we had a recession in this country, and the extent of the foreign control of the economy has been increasing year by year by year.
The Minister of Finance and the ministry of finance refuse to learn the lesson that these things simply do not work in terms of the economy, let alone in terms of the fairness of the tax system. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that Canada was the last country in the western world to impose a capital gains tax. We were told over the years that the reason we could not have a capital gains tax in this country was that if we did it would slow down the economy at a time when we were trying to influence Canadians to own more of Canada. However, the appearance of the capital gains tax did not prevent our having cyclical recessions and having the economy more and more under foreign control.
None of these measures has worked. The reason is that they are blunt instruments. They hit all the economy and all elements of the economy, instead of hitting at the particular problem which the economy faces. If we need measures to deal with the fact the the Americans are determined to pull jobs back to the United States and out of Canada, you will not do it by reducing the income tax rate in respect of the corporations, because if the United States is determined to do that it will find some other way. After you have cut the income tax rate from 49 per cent to 40 per cent, the Americans in Washington will think of something else in answer to this. What will the Minister of Finance do? If he cuts the income tax rate from 40 per cent to 30 per cent, then they will think of something else. This is a silly way in which to attack the problem, because when you decrease the income tax payable by the corporations, that decrease is not translated into a decrease in prices but, rather, is translated into an increase in the profits of the corporations.
This is a silly way to do it because you never catch up with what they do in the United States. If that becomes a problem there are direct ways to deal with it. The direct way is by saying to the Americans that we are not a weak country, that we are not standing on our knees before them, and that if they are going to take steps to cripple the economy of Canada we will take steps to make sure that they do not cripple it.
There are all sorts of ways to do that. I suspect that the direct way of insisting that the production be Canadian in

June 13, 1973
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
various industries might accomplish something in counteracting the measures in Washington, whereas the income tax cut will accomplish nothing in that regard and will merely give the corporations a further addition to their profits. Their profits have been phenomenal. What kind of justice permits this parliament, this government and the Tories in this House to hand more profits to the corporations at this time? Corporate profits increased 16 per cent in 1971 over 1970. They increased 20 per cent in 1972 over 1971, and in the first quarter of this year they increased at an annual rate of 53 per cent over 1972.
The Minister of Finance and the Tories are in agreement that we should adopt measures in this House which would increase the profits of the corporations, measures which according to the Minister of Finance on May 8, 1972, will cost the federal treasury $500 million, at a time when the corporations are making this level of profits. If there is any threat internationally to be met, then they have a sufficient profit margin to be able to meet it out of their existing profits. It is morally absolutely wrong to add to their profits at the expense of the ordinary Canadian taxpayer.
I come back to what I said when I believe the minister, I am sure unavoidably, was absent from the House. I was saying that this is the wrong anticyclical measure. If corporate profits were on the way down, then there might be some sense-I am not at all sure there would even then be sense-in increasing the profits of the corporations with the thought that we would be doing something good for the Canadian economy. Surely, however, there is no sense at all, in terms of elementary economics, to increasing the profits of corporations and to increasing the availability of disposal income in their hands at a time when according to the minister and his government the economy is heating up.
We must be careful about how much we give the individual taxpayer and how much we allow the interest rate to go up, not by putting the foot on the brake, as I think the Prime Minister once said, but by keeping it very lightly on the gas pedal. What he is doing in this bill is the exact opposite to what he is doing in every other area of the economy. That is simply wrong. In economic terms it is unacceptable. In social terms and, in my view, in moral terms, it is unforgivable to do what is now proposed before us, because at the same time that corporate profits went up 20 per cent in 1972 over 1971 and 16 per cent in
1971	over 1970, total labour income in this country increased 10 per cent in 1971 and only 11 per cent in 1972. And when you deal with total labour income you are not dealing merely with the lower echelons of labour but with the total income, which includes presidents of corporations, vice-presidents and managers of corporations and all wage and salary earners in this country. That increased by only 10 per cent and 11 per cent compared to 16 per cent and 20 per cent respectively for 1971 and 1972.
When you look at the manufacturing industry, the industry the minister now wants to help with more profits, you find that the average rate of earnings in manufacturing rose 8.6 per cent in 1971 over 1970 and 7.9 per cent in
1972	over 1971-and we are prepared to give these manufacturing and processing industries a further $500 million of the taxpayers' money. We cannot buy that. It is not

glittering rhetoric or any other kind qf rhetoric; it is simply that our policy or approach is oriented against the idea that what the corporations want the corporations get. This has been the policy of the Liberals and the Conservatives for 100 years. What the corporations, the big boys, demand, the big boys get every time in every way, or take it if they do not get it. But the ordinary taxpayer in Canada, when he demands just some kind of equity or justice gets a crumb, as he did in the February, 1973, budget. He did not get as much as was given to the corporations.
I want to deal with the review mechanism. I said earlier in my remarks that obviously as a result of what my party said and what I as its leader said inside parliament, outside parliament and in conversation which he and I once had about the general situation, the Minister of Finance became convinced that we would not support this bill, these tax concessions, no matter how packaged and no matter what the consequences.
Even at the time when the Conservative Party was more anxious to have an election than they appear to be now, we took exactly the same position no matter what the consequences. He looked for a way of winning support elsewhere, and I do not condemn him for that. That is the way to survive in a minority parliament. And if on several occasions the government looked to our support-I make no bones about it-we were glad to give it. They have just as much right to look for support in another direction if our support is not available. However, so far as I am concerned I do not buy this review mechanism, for several reasons. First, I hope the hon. member for Peace River and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who is not here but may read what I say, or may be informed-
He is with the president of General Motors.

-will not take offence when I say that I never bought this statement of the Leader of the Opposition that he did not want this to be a permanent part of the tax system. That always sounded very hollow to me because there is nothing that is a permanent part of the tax system. We have at least one budget each year-in the last few years we have had two and three budgets a year- and every time there is a budget the tax system is changed in some way. I never bought that statement of the Leader of the Opposition and I am not at all sure how deep it came from the heart of the hon. gentleman. It is silly to talk about anything being a permanent part of the tax system when the tax system is changed with every budget at least every year and sometimes two or three times a year. But it gave the Minister of Finance an opening.
And he took it.

The Leader of the Opposition, having made a statement which the Minister of Finance knew perfectly well had no meaning and no relevance to the fiscal system of this country, the minister or his colleagues or he and his colleagues, said, "We have that guy now. He does not want it to be a permanent part of the system. He says he wants it to end on December 31, 1973. We will tell him that we
