will have a monitoring system, and next April 1 60 of his members can demand a review and if it is carried then it will become law". The Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Peace River said today, "You bought my idea. Now we are ready to support you. I made a meaningless and irrelevant statement and you were sensible enough to pick it up. Let us shake hands. We are again together as we always have been and as we ought to be". But it is a gimmick and it is a dangerous gimmick. It is an essential part of our kind of parliamentary system that the initiative for taxation, for fiscal policies, for budgetary policies is the initiative of the government. The Minister of Finance, in order to survive, is ready to leave it to the initiative of 60 backbench members to decide.
I also have no use for it because that kind of gimmickry will sometimes hit us in the face. The Canadian people are not unintelligent, even when they vote against my party. They use their intelligence and I have great respect for them. They will recognize this as a gimmick created only for the purpose of keeping the Liberal government in office. That kind of gimmick is no good.
Wait till 9.45 tomorrow night, David, and see where you are; see how you vote.

Since you are being impolite enough not to speak through Mr. Speaker but to me directly, I will be impolite enough, George, not to speak through Mr. Speaker and tell you that you will see where we are and it will not be a further attempt of the Conservative Party to talk through both sides of its mouth at the same time.
Hear, hear!

I said earlier that we are determined to do our best to make this parliament work. There are a good many things that we hope this parliament will accomplish and we will co-operate with all members of parliament to accomplish those things. This is worse than a gimmick. I am sorry that I must say this, and I am not saying it to offend or to insult anybody, but I cannot trust a review that is carried out by the Department of Finance itself. I cannot trust it because they are the people who have presented these policies for God knows how many years. They are the people who have been convinced about the value of fast write-offs and income tax cuts for corporations, and suddenly they will be the people who will become so objective as to eat their own words and their own ideas and ignore their own prejudices. Like the devil! No one does that; no one can do that.
People who for years have been responsible for a policy cannot be trusted with a review of the same policy. You do not need to be a genius to see that. If you went into an industry, a factory or any office and asked the people responsible for the policies and direction of that industry to make a review as to whether the policies they have always supported are good, you would not get an objective opinion.
Therefore, I think that this so-called monitoring or review is worth nothing. When the Minister of Finance tells me that it will be objective, that it will be based on facts and figures, I say I have lived long enough to know exactly what that means. The person who arranges the agenda sets the tone. The way in which you write up a fact
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
sets the tone. The way in which you arrange the figures in a column and the way in which you set up the various columns sets the tone. There is no objectivity in that sense. They will not be facts and figures; they will be facts and figures as seen through the eyes of people who have always been committed to the policies which they are now supposed to monitor, review and judge. I cannot have any confidence in that kind of review.
The Minister of Finance makes a great deal of the fact that small businesses will have a reduction in the income tax rate of 25 per cent to 20 per cent. If his bill were limited to that or if it were limited to a reduction in the income tax rate to Canadian-owned firms only, then we might have taken a look at that bill; but in reality the small Canadian businessman will only get crumbs out of this. He will get a 20 per cent income tax rate instead of a 25 per cent rate if he has less than $50,000 in profits, if my memory serves me right and I am pretty sure it does. So you take 5 per cent of $40,000, if he makes a $40,000 profit, which comes to $2,000, as against 9 per cent of $100 million profit for the large corporation, or a $10 million profit.
The Minister of Finance is comparing the elephant and the rabbit, and he thinks he has got us in a corner because of the little crumb he offers the small Canadian businessman. If he is prepared to change his bill so that the income tax concession-this does not have anything to do with the fast write-offs, because they are of no use at all-is limited only to Canadiafi-owned firms, then one might look at it because then it might have some value in promoting Canadian ownership as against the multinational corporations that control over 60 per cent of our manufacturing and, although I have not seen this figure and I can be corrected if I am wrong, I venture to suggest control over 80 per cent of our processing in Canada.
I feel strongly about this because, for the reasons I have given, in our view these concessions to the corporations will not do anything for the economy, will not promote employment and will only increase their profit. I feel strongly about this because of the things that I see $500 million could do for the ordinary people of Canada. I said this the other day and I make no apology for repeating it: $500 million is $100 million more than the increase we have given to the old age pensioners and the adjustment in the cost of living allowance for old age pensioners; $500 million, if we could spare it from the federal treasury, could give another $10 to $20 a month to the old age pensioners of this country.
We have been waiting for weeks for legislation to deal with disability pensions for veterans. It is obvious that there must be quarrels inside the cabinet as to how high the increase should be and whether or not the cabinet should accept the report of the committee which suggested that the escalation should be on the basis of the cost of living. I have not made the calculation but I am certain that $200 million out of this $500 million could give the disabled veterans the kind of pension that would enable them to live in the dignity which their service warrants. We are also waiting with baited breath for legislation that will increase the family allowance to an average of $20 per child. It took months and months to decide to do this. With

$300 million out of this $500 million we could make family allowances of $30 per child.
When on February 19 of this year the minister gave an income tax cut to individual taxpayers on a progressive basis-and we were delighted with the fact that it was progressive-he made the minimum $100. As I calculate it, Mr. Speaker, another $300 million or $400 million would enable him to give a minimum of $150 in the personal income tax cut.
It is for these reasons, because we cannot see any validity in the economic arguments presented by the minister and because we believe it is socially wrong and unjust to give the corporations further concessions, that we will oppose this bill on second reading and throughout all its stages.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us is the result, we all know, of pre-election measures, proposed as long ago as 1972 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), though of course the October 30 election results had not been foreseen then.
Since that time the minister has been beating about the bush in an attempt to rally the Progressive Conservatives to his side, since he is sure of the very clear stand that has always been taken by our friends in the New Democratic Party. I can understand that the minister found himself in a dilemma, and his evasiveness this afternoon shows that we are now witnessing a three-way family fight, between the Liberal Party, the New Democratic Party and the Progressive Conservatives, and perhaps this session will pass into history as the one during which we were constantly involved in the old eternal triangle.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, we are not concerned with such petty matters, for if the Progressive Conservatives go back to the untenable position which they adopted at the beginning of the session, it will be proof of a rather flagrant lack of responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, early in this session the Progressive Conservatives had but one concern, and that was to defeat the government. And when faced with a measure which normally would have received their full support, they thought it wise to say that they were going to oppose it, which, of course, bothered the government, but it also bothered the Progressive Conservative party. In view of all that has been going on in this House for the past few months, in my opinion we are still the freest since we are not tied down in any way and can express in the freest possible manner what people think, what they dearly want, and we therefore wish to encourage the government to consider the very constructive and positive criticisms we have made.
Once again, in his speech, the minister explained his purpose in introducing this bill; by reducing corporate taxes he hopes to remedy the effects of three categories of problems: first, those caused by the devaluation and revaluation of the dollar, as well as by the increase in the value of foreign currencies; second, the problems caused by the need for our industries to compete with foreign production; and third, which may be his strongest argument, the need to create new jobs.

Mr. Speaker, we have always opposed an economic and financial system that leads to impossible situations. As our proposals are always turned down, we are forced to say whether we agree or not with proposals to be applied to what we consider to be an inadequate system.
We would like to be as optimistic as the minister and think that this bill will have all the positive effects he referred to but we know that is impossible in the current economic system. We are prepared to allow the government to give it a try, particularly since it guarantees us that the House will have certain prerogatives allowing it to ask almost anytime for the suspension of that law if it proved inefficient.
But, Mr. Speaker, in spite of all that we insist on restating the necessary points. In his first point the minister said that tax reductions can favour competition. Mr. Speaker, when a country like ours builds its economy on 52 per cent of the value of goods manufactured for exportation, when the Canadian consumer buys around 70 to 80 per cent foreign products, this is a ridiculous situation.
How come we are compelled to base our production volume on exports, while as consumers we must rely on foreign products? There is something incomprehensible.
It is the same when we refer to exchange rates. When the common market countries or the United States decide to devaluate or revaluate their currency, we are affected.
If our entire economy is based on exports, it is then agreed that we lie at the mercy of anything which may happen throughout the world. This is why we suggest, as members of the Social Credit, that all those questions would be minor issues if we implemented an adequate economic system and if the concern of the government were truly the same as that of the Canadian people. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that all Canadians would like to manufacture here everything which can materially be produced. The only conditions are to have the necessary raw materials, sufficient manpower and of course the required talent, that is individuals capable of drawing up plans and carrying them out. This is necessary to manufacture any item.
Now, if we were to apply this simple principle of making financially possible what is physically feasible, we could not only settle our economic and financial problems but also create employment because if we buy abroad the best part of our consumer goods, it is obvious that in the meantime we shall keep a countless number of workers on our unemployment roll. This is self-explanatory.
But if we were to apply logical and sound economic principles, we would never be faced with those problems since production cost would not matter. If we are physically in a position to manufacture such or such kind of products-and I know that in Canada we can produce just about anything-it would then be sufficient to balance the value of this production with the purchasing power of people. There would never be any inflation since the value of the money representing the purchasing power would be equal to the products that would exist. Therefore, such a system would never breed inflation. A system of that kind is extremely simple.
But as I repeated on many occasions, the simplest things are sometimes the most difficult to explain. And this is a problem especially for us, Creditistes, who must try to
June 13, 1973

make people understand very simple things that they will not admit at all.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we certainly have reservations about this bill, considering it applies to the present economic system. Of course, as a matter of principle we believe precisely that taxes should be reduced to their simplest form. As a matter of principle, I repeat, we are against tax increases and we are also, as a matter of principle, in favour of tax reductions. Since the bill deals with a tax reduction, as a matter of principle, we perfectly agree with that.
But we are reluctant to believe that this measures will have all the results hoped for. Why? Because this is not the first time a reduction has been suggested. There was one in 1971 and others before that. What were the results of corporate tax cuts? As far as I know, the unemployment rate increased last year. That is why we entertain some reservations as regards the effects this bill could have, even though, in principle, we are in favour of lessening the corporate financial burden.
In spite of negative critics, we want to emphasize the positive aspect which could be considered. I mentioned earlier a principle which our party would like to see implemented, namely that of making financially possible what is physically feasible.
If we want to settle once and for all the persistent problem of inflation, unemployment and production, in brief if we truly want to find adequate solutions, we should, for example, consider the best way to helping the corporations affected by this bill. Shall we succeed in solving this problem by granting corporations more substantial tax reliefs or should we subsidize them as the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is doing? No, Mr. Speaker, because it might be difficult to do justice to everybody if we were to allow a substantial tax cut for a few companies.
We know that it may be quite easy to hide a large part of net income; thus, the tax returns of companies cannot be trusted sometimes. There might be-I do not suggest that this will necessarily happen-some injustice but this would not create any problem if the Canadian taxpayer were not called upon to promote the expansion of a company thanks to his own money, either through a tax cut, as provided for in this bill, or through grants. In both cases, we must remind ourselves that personal income tax represent 80 per cent of over-all taxes, Mr. Speaker. The people pay for it, they will have to pay for it, either through income tax or through taxes of all kinds. And when grants are given, the same thing happens: taxpayers are again expected to pick up the tab.
If the principle were applied that any new production can and must be financed through new credit, the problem would be solved because, if a business needs to be assisted, the most basic assistance it would need would be credit, and if credit was facilitated, the company involved would be responsible for the value of its loan. Thus, the taxpayer would not be directly obliged to help it.
I suggest that this would be much more logical and besides, a business should have the opportunity of choosing between two means I am going to point out right now.
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
Let us take the example of a small business which needs $100,000. It will apply for a grant from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The department grants a maximum of $25,000. Where to get the remaining $75,000, Mr. Speaker? Of course, there is the money market where it is possible to borrow at 93A, 10 or 11 per cent and maybe more. Because of the increase in the Bank of Canada interest rate as announced this week, we can expect one every bank to follow suit. At that time, the businessman must make a choice between-and this is my assumption-taking the $25,000 from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and get the $75,000 he needs at an interest rate of 12 per cent. What happens? A recurrence of what happened since that policy was adopted, and a good deal of business receiving grants are going bankrupt. Why? Because they cannot even finance the cost of their loan.
Let us now look at the other alternative. If instead of giving a grant of $25,000 and having the rest financed at 12 per cent, the loan covers the $100,000 that is needed by that business but at an interest rate of 2 or 3 per cent plus cost of the loan itself, what will the industrialist do? We know the answer. Instead of the grant of $25,000 and the loan at 12 per cent, he will prefer to have the total credit of $100,000 at an interest rate which will allow him to expand his business, increase the number of products, create a lot of jobs and give consumers in general a greater purchasing power to buy his products. That is the way to spin the wheel as it should be and as it should have always been.
I think that rather than tax exemptions we should be considering the possibility of facilitating access to credit on the basis of the principle that it is absolutely normal that new productions be financed through new credits.
There is also another very positive way which goes against what was proposed by the minister when he said that those tax exemptions are aimed at making it easier for foreign competition. If only someone would accept the proposition that it is not necessary, not useful and sometimes ridiculous to base our whole way of life, our whole economic system, on foreigners! It is not rational, particularly in a rich country like Canada. There is another way, Mr. Speaker, and it is through a compensated discount. When we cannot manufacture some products in Canada, the reason is not that we are short of raw materials, manpower or know-how, but simply that some other country can produce them at lower cost. It is foolish to yield to those circumstances and let our industries die because of that.
Take industries such as textiles in Quebec which have to close down or considerably reduce their production only because we are invaded by textile products from Japan, China or other countries. Mr. Speaker, it is ridiculous when we know that they are one of our most important industries. It is possible to cope with that situation simply by giving a compensated discount which could be used to compete with foreign countries and God knows that those countries can do the same in other ways.
I for one have serious doubts when buying a foreign product as to whether it was cheaper to manufacture. I find it hard to believe that, Mr. Speaker, especially when we know that in Quebec particularly wages are not so high and they are much lower than those paid in the United

States. It is difficult for me to admit that the United States for instance can make a product at lower cost than in Quebec; that is not always the truth.
Moreover, we are not there to control their production and the policy of their government. So we have only one thing to do; mind our own business. We should be able to control all foreign products; we know what we can produce ourselves and as regards products which would be more expensive-yet essential-we would only have to give the consumer a compensated discount for interested producers.
Mr. Speaker, when we consider the whole problem of tax cuts, we are faced with the problem of the economy as a whole. We hear over and over again that inflation is the cause of all of that.
At a given time, unemployment increases because of the fight against inflation. Another time, if the government reduces its budgetary expenses, it is again because of inflation, and if there is some change in the exchange rate, it is again because of inflation.
I have before me an article from issues 3 and 4 of the periodical Le reveil du consommateur, dealing with inflation, and I think it should be quoted, so that once and for all people will stop being afraid of words which can mean almost anything. I shall quote from this article later on.
People are told to tighten their belt because of inflation. I am sure that the farmer at the back of beyond does not understand anything because he sees his carrots and his trees growing and his cows giving milk as usual. He does not understand that because of inflation, he should have to tighten his belt.
I will read from the article I mentioned earlier, by Mr. Normand Brouillet, and I quote:
Does inflation serve the workers' interests? After this brief review of the origins and causes of the persistent inflation which characterizes our economy, after finding that to a certain extent governments have to choose between a reasonable inflation rate and high unemployment on the one hand, or a faster rate of increase in prices with less unemployment, which causes demand to rise or decline, it remains to be determined which economical situation is less detrimental to the workers. In the present situation, we believe that inflation is mainly a reflection of the framework within which workers and management are fighting to grab the largest possible share of national revenue. We believe that inflation is more beneficial to the workers' interests than severe unemployment. First, because unemployed have no real purchasing power in a society such as ours. They are isolated and have no possibility of exploiting their only economical force, namely their work capacity.
This is similar to what we say when we promote anything which might increase the individual's purchasing power and we are not afraid of inflation; as evidence of it I am continuing the quotation:
Thus, inflation makes it possible, not only for employed workers to continue improving their standard of living, but for an even larger number of workers (since the unemployment rate is generally lower in periods of inflation) to benefit by the growth in the national economy.
Mr. Speaker, to conclude, I shall now quote an extract from the same publication, which is taken from a book entitled "Les consequences de l'inflation: mythes et rea-

lites" (the consequences of inflation: myth and reality) bv M. J. Depatie:
In short, inflation does not seem to us to be as disastrous for all workers as we are too often asked to believe. For indeed, those who lose the most are those who have lent money, who see the absolute value of their loans decreasing. Now in our system the lenders are the banks, the trust companies, the finance companies, and so on .. . They are those who have an interest in seeing that inflation is kept a minimum. Basically, it is for the benefit of this minority that the government combats inflation so vigorously, since even the production sector can adjust to cost hikes by corresponding price hikes.
Mr. Speaker, the time has come for us to say a few elementary truths of which we are aware, as everyone else is; certain rumors are kept alive which circulate among the people and get on their nerves. That is why unemployment was finally accepted, and all sorts of inefficient measure justified.
For instance, when we ask why old age pensions are not paid people of 60, we are told it would cost a billion dollars to do so. And what of it considering the potential of this country to produce goods worth hundreds of billions? Why not place a billion dollars' worth more purchasing power in the people's hands?
Mr. Speaker, the time has come to set up real priorities in the field of economics and, in closing, I would like to express my agreement with the Minister of Finances when he says that corporate tax reductions will encourage the creation of new jobs and produce all sorts of good things for the country. I am willing to accept that, and I hope it comes true. That is why I am not against Bill C-192, though I know full well that it will not solve any of the fundamental problems we have to face. To remedy the situation, sound and logical economic principles, such as we propose, should be applied.

Mr. Speaker, this bill has been a long time coming to this stage, much too long for the business community. It was rather interesting watching the cat-and-mouse game the government played with this bill. In almost every weekly edition of certain financial papers there were references to the tax bill; it was coming, it was not coming, there was a division in the cabinet, we would have it next week or next month. We finally have it in a somewhat modified form.
The government has kept those in the business community who will benefit from this bill in a state of anticipation. Some whom I have talked to felt at one stage that the bill would be withdrawn. Others thought it was buried so far down the legislative list it would never reach parliament. I more or less made the same prediction. I had reservations about the way it was being handled. I did not know whether the minister was really serious when he talked about the effect it would have and the help it would give to industry.
There was so much rhetoric on the bill before it was introduced that a great number of Canadian businessmen are convinced they are going to receive a tax cut. I am not referring to manufacturers or processors. I talked to a number of these businessmen in my constituency and other areas. They are of the opinion they will get a tax cut even though they are not manufacturers or distributors. The truth is that most Canadian businesses other than

manufacturers or distributors will receive a tax increase. That is one of the faults of this bill.
Looking at the rate of inflation and the increase in the bank rate, I wonder how effective the tax reduction will be, in real terms, to industry. The minister said he is concerned about the financial status of Canadian industry. I find that a bit hard to swallow. If he had been really concerned, this bill would have been introduced in 1972 or at least a couple of months ago.
Why did we have to wait until three weeks ago to receive the analysis on the full impact of the DISC legislation from the Canadian Tax Foundation? It is rather significant that we had to wait this period of time. DISC has been in operation for 18 or 24 months. I believe this analysis was prepared by the Canadian Tax Foundation and sent in by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. The minister said today that this is one of the great cornerstones in the bill to reduce the corporate tax rate.
The minister stated that the long-term effects of DISC will be disastrous to Canadian industry. However, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) said in committee that he does not know of any Canadian industry that has been injured as a result of the DISC legislation. It is rather difficult to reconcile those two statements. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) based much of his argument on the DISC legislation. If the Minister of Finance is so concerned about our primary and secondary industries, why is he allowing the bank rate to escalate? Why does he not put a check on inflation so that the real effect of the tax cut can be utilized by industries, particularly those involved in export?
We seem to be dealing in half measures. I would like to hear the minister say we are going to have a tax rate equal to the lowest effective tax rate of any industrialized nation in our trading sphere. In other words, I would like to hear him say that we will be competitive with any nation of the world on matters of tax as far as our industry is concerned. If the minister brought forward a broad tax philosophy like that, people would be very pleased provided it was across the board and covered all industries, not only manufacturers and processors.
The minister does not seem to have any concern for the transportation industry. These people are not going to benefit from the tax cuts. As a matter of fact, in most cases they will have a tax increase. Here is an industry that is so vital to the economy, yet no relief is given to it.
As a matter of fact, the truck transportation industry, the "for hire" industry, is in a very serious position this year. Most truckers compete with the railways and they are now facing a situation where taxation has increased, fuel prices are going up, and they are caught in the inflationary spiral. It appears that the railways are considering some form of subsidy this year, which means that the transportation industry will raise freight rates, the cost of which will be passed on to manufacturing industry. So where will we go from there? The whole situation makes the tax reduction somewhat non-effective.
I am also concerned about the position of the service industry. The American service industry is included within the DISC legislation. Some U.S. consulting firms
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
and engineering companies are bidding in Canada in competition with Canadian companies, using the benefits of the DISC legislation to the detriment of Canadian corporations in the same field. Yet no concern is shown for these corporations which form a vital part of our industrial complex.
The special write-off provisions and depreciation features are good and in general we agree with them. The big problem facing our industry as time goes on, once the back of unemployment is broken, is the productivity of industry vis-a-vis world trade. We have to be ever mindful of productivity and must have available legislation which sees to it that industry has the necessary machinery to remain productive. Other countries, such as Germany, Japan and the United States and most of the western European nations have had features like this in their business law for many years, certainly since the last war. I hope that after the two-year period has expired we will re-examine the situation and reintroduce these provisions.
The definition in the bill of "manufacturing and processing" has caused a good deal of concern to many of us. Today I received a copy of a document headed "Proposed income tax regulation, manufacturing and processing profits". It is rather interesting to note the document is dated December 28, 1972, and was released on Friday, January 8, 1973. In this document are some horrendous definitions of business activities, to say nothing of complicated formulae which I have shown to a couple of chartered accountants who told me they could not figure them out and would have to take a real, long look at them.
One matter we must look at very seriously is this: we must realize many of our industries are engaged in manufacturing, service and retail and it will be very difficult to segregate these industries for the purpose of taxation. It would have been much easier to apply this legislation across the board to all Canadian industries and companies.
A very interesting article appeared in yesterday's Ottawa Journal about the service business. I should like to quote a few extracts:
Service business is big business.
Over the next decade, three out of every four jobs created will be in the service industries. . . . service workers will outnumber employees in manufacturing and natural resources industries by better than two to one.
Within the service area itself, the rapidly rising demand for utilities, transportation and communication services far outstrips growth for other private and public services.
Lagging productivity in services is the principal factor triggering inflationary spending increases. In many service occupations it creates insatiable manpower demands which the consumer pays through rapidly rising prices.
Companies originally devoted to retailing have integrated backward into manufacturing and a large national retailer in Canada now offers a repair department as well as financial counselling, selling life insurance and mutual funds.
So there will be some very difficult divisions to be made in some of these industries. I can think of several large nationally-known industries producing brand name products who have manufacturing service and retail segments within their businesses. How the proposed formula will sort them out is beyond me, and I shall be interested to hear a little more detail in this regard. What I am fright-

Income Tax Act (No. 2)
ened of is another section or empire being spawned in the Department of Finance as a result of this bill, with a group of experts and people running around the country trying to figure out for the manufacturer which slot he should drop into.
Generally speaking, I think we are going to vote to send this bill to committee. However, in committee we will want to carefully examine the review process mechanism and see it tightened up. I think it is fair to say that on that particular point we will take a hard line. I think the minister has been put on notice that when the bill goes to committee we are going to lay hard on this review process and see that some real meaning is given to it. That is something to which we will be looking forward.
I think the definitions relating to manufacturing and processing are going to drive the average businessman of the kind I know in small industries and secondary industries, right up the wall. Let me just illustrate to the House what I mean. According to the document I have referred to-
The manufacturing and processing profits of such a corporation for a taxation year will be that proportion of its Canadian active business income for the year which its manufacturing labour plus manufacturing capital is of its total labour plus total capital for the year.
After you have swallowed that, Mr. Speaker, you are given a formula which expresses the foregoing as MP- which is "manufacturing profit" equals ML MC over TL TC h- ABI. If we thought Bill C-259 had problems, I think when the business community takes issue with this one the minister will see some backlash he has not anticipated. When we get into committee we can talk to the figure filberts and the other philosophers who put this formula together and defined the various categories of manufacturing and pricing to see whether we can get them defined in terms that every businessman who is struggling for the buck in a competitive market can understand.
There is disappointment that the minister has chosen to favour only one segment of the business community of this country. I do not know how we can talk about an industrial strategy unless we consider all industries in our business community. It is not fair to leave out the service industry, the transportation industry, the consulting engineers and others in our business community, including large retail merchants. It is not fair that they should be exempted from these tax reduction provisions. I would suggest to the minister that if in his wisdom he had seen fit to include the business community across the board in this tax legislation, it might well have been in operation months ago. I do not think there would have been any holding back or waiting for the proper time to introduce it, just before a parliamentary recess.
Let me say in closing that we are going to vote for this bill on second reading so that we can take a long look at it in committee. We are going to chew hard at the review procedure and lean pretty heavily on tightening it up, because we think it needs tightening up. The minister has been given notice that we are going to consider the formula we see here and try to get some of the language put

on a level where the guy who makes the buck can understand what he is contributing;.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to comment on the remarks of the leader of the NDP (Mr. Lewis). I noted that he seemed quite disturbed about his presumption that the party to which I belong was going to support this bill on second reading in order that it be sent to the committee. He said that the monitoring process which had been suggested by the minister was in fact not realistic and would not be objective. He said monitoring is worth nothing. He said the way you write up the facts sets the tone; the way you set up the game sets the tone. In short, he said there would be no objectivity in the minister's monitoring because they propose to monitor the force of the manufacturing and processing companies themselves. He also said that we cannot trust a review carried out by the ministry itself.
Perhaps the leader of that party is missing the fundamental fact that at some point in a confrontation or debate it is wrong to hit a man when he is down. When we consider the history of this matter we find that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) started out very confidently on May 8, 1972. He was less confident in February, 1973, and I believe he has virtually conceded his position as of now. If he feels, because of his current attitude and misgivings concerning the actual effect of his tax measures, that the government now needs a monitoring system, this parliament should at least co-operate to the extent of letting him off the hook so that the monitoring system he proposes to set up will be meaningful.
I think we must remember the statements of the Minister of Finance concerning the proposed tax legislation when he introduced this measure on May 8, 1972. He said one of the purposes was to-
-protect existing jobs and provide well-paying new jobs for Canadians in and near the urban centres where they want to work.
Subsequently, I asked the minister questions when he appeared before the committee of this House and found that he was very much less explicit as to what, in fact, they anticipated to be the job-creation impact of these tax measures. I asked this direct question:
How many jobs do you feel you can attribute directly to the proposed tax reduction and to the fast write-off?
The minister replied:
That is impossible to calculate.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, this minister has repeatedly told the press, the people of Canada and the members of this House that he knows his tax measures are going to have a job-creation effect. When he is asked to be specific, he tells us it is impossible to calculate that effect. I suggest that means the minister and the cabinet are now having serious doubts and concerns about the real impact of these tax measures. I have in mind that question as to how many businesses in Canada will be affected by this rather vague term "manufacturing and processing". I should like to know what businesses in Canada will be affected. Again, when questioned in the committee the minister and his deputies were unable to come up with any specific calculations as to the number of businesses in Canada which would actually benefit from these tax measures.

I found it very alarming that the minister was unable to come up with any specific figure as to the extent foreign-controlled corporations in Canada would benefit from the tax measures. This is something members of this House should not overlook. The minister has made representations in the House that this is going to be beneficial to processing and manufacturing concerns in the country and that it will have the direct advantage of creating jobs, yet when he is pinned down to giving specifics he can only reply that it is impossible to be specific on the subject.
I suggest that when he throws out the figure, as he did on May 8, 1972, of $500 million in a full year as the amount the government will forgo in revenue, we cannot rely on that figure. He admitted specifically in the committee that he himself did not know. How can he be sure, even using the word "about", that the government will forgo $500 million in respect of this tax measure?
The fact is that the government, for its own good reasons, on May 8, 1972, made the decision to introduce the tax measures which are finally before us today. I believe the government now has serious doubts as to whether it took the proper course, but it feels it has no alternative, for face-saving purposes-call it what you want-but to persist in its adamant stand that in some form these tax measures must proceed through this House.
That is why I feel it is important to first comment on the speech made by the Leader of the New Democratic Party because, like us, he is disturbed about the proposed operation of the monitoring authority. We have our doubts. We believe that the proper thing, however, is to at least give the bill second reading and allow it to pass to the committee, where we will ask some hard questions which we will want answered in a more direct and factual way than the way in which the minister has answered questions put to him to the present time in the committee concerning the impact of these tax measures.
Another point raised by our colleague the leader of the NDP was the question of what he calls a rip-off or sell-out to business. I think it is odd that he did not make clear, or at least I did not get it from his remarks, that the tax measure introduced by the Minister of Finance actually increases taxation for most businessmen in this country. This is one of the fundamental fallacies in the tax approach of the Minister of Finance. He is showing favouritism within the business community without being able to demonstrate to this House, to the economists or to the people of Canada, that his favouritism in the form of tax reductions and fast write-offs in respect of the manufacturing and processing fields will actually produce results in accordance with any foregone target or objective.
With regard to whether in fact the bulk of the Canadian businessmen will be paying higher taxes, this question was answered by the Minister of Finance, again at the committee hearings to which I referred, but only after extremely hard questioning. He took every opportunity to avoid admitting that most businesses in Canada will not be paying less taxation in the current year, 1973, but will be paying more. I am pleased to tell members that after about 24 questions having been put to him in which he tried to evade the question, he finally gave the answer.
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
I asked the minister what rate would be paid in 1973 by businesses other than in the manufacturing and processing fields, and he said that it would be 49 per cent. I then said that such a person would pay 49 per cent and last year he paid 46.5 per cent. The minister finally agreed. He said that last year it was 46.5 per cent. Surely this type of deceit is not expected from the Minister of Finance in a country such as Canada. I suggest that this is something which should have been pointed out by the leader of the NDP instead of the broad-brush approach which he likes to take in respect of the big corporations by saying they are getting some type of tax concession. Surely it would have been much more direct for him to have pointed out that a segment of the business community is getting a concession, but that some businessmen in 1973 are actually being called upon to pay more in taxation than they did last year.
Having said that, I believe it would not be wise on our part to oppose the bill, certainly at second reading stage. If the government is having serious doubts, and I suggest it is, concerning the actual effect of this tax measure, it is natural it should want to have a monitoring system, and I believe it is the job of this House to ensure that the monitoring system that is set up will be objective and will get to the facts. I also suggest that if it is objective and gets to the facts, it will prove what my leader and members of this party have said for some time, that this is an unsatisfactory measure to have been brought in at this time in this country.
I believe the minister has made a significant concession. Let us look at the history. In May, 1972, there was no suggestion of any monitoring at all. I sat in this House on February 19, 1973, and remember many members chuckling and laughing when the minister started down the path of looking squarely at the NDP and saying he had now decided to have a monitoring system in order, presumably, to satisfy somebody that these measures will have the proper effect. Not too long ago we sat in this House and heard the final concession, that not only would there be a monitoring system but there would also be an interim report giving us an opportunity, under the new legislation, to challenge the continuation of the existence of this tax if 60 members or more of this House saw fit. How far can one expect a man to go without actually conceding he was wrong on May 8?
I say it is wrong for us to keep pounding on this issue when the government realizes it has made a mistake. Rather than making so much of the fact that it is not 30 members who would bring in this resolution but 60, I think the NDP should have made the point that according to the facts which are before not only this House but the public, it may well be that if the present government is in power in April next year it will be the first to move to get this type of taxation provision out of our system and not allow it to continue. That point perhaps has been overlooked in this debate. People like to save face. This government is particularly anxious to remain in power, and if it is to remain in power it will obviously want to save face on this issue.
